analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agents to get a judge's warrant before using state and local surveillance data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 15, 2026 with 7 Republican cosponsors and referred to two House committees, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill stops federal law enforcement from quietly pulling license plate scans, camera footage, long-range audio, and similar data collected by state and local police without first getting a warrant from a federal judge. It sets limits on how long that data can be kept, blocks evidence obtained without a warrant from being used in federal trials, requires public reports on how often the data is used, and bars most federal money from buying the listed surveillance devices. It also lets people sue federal agencies that violate the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose movements, conversations, and locations are recorded by the growing network of license plate readers and police cameras operated by state and local agencies, and who currently have no way of knowing when a federal agency pulls those records. It also protects anyone investigated by federal law enforcement, by barring warrantless data from federal trials and requiring the government to disclose it to the defense.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone recorded by local police cameras and plate readers

how_it_helps.text: Federal law enforcement agencies may not access, query, or task state and local surveillance data without a warrant issued by a federal judge, closing a path around warrant requirements [S2].
Data obtained without a warrant cannot be used as evidence in federal court, and the government must still disclose it to the defendant under standard criminal discovery and Brady rules [S2].

The Attorney General must publish a 'Jurisdictional Wall List' of covered technologies — including automated license plate readers, occupant cameras, continuous-coverage cameras, and long-range microphones — reviewed every 90 days [S2].
Federal funds generally cannot be used to buy or install the listed surveillance devices, with carve-outs for toll systems, school violence prevention, and case-bounded warrant-based police use [S2].

Individuals whose data was taken in violation of the law can sue federal agencies for damages and injunctive relief, with sovereign immunity waived, and agencies must keep audit records and report uses to Congress and the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies, which would lose warrant-free access to a large pool of state and local surveillance data and face new record-keeping, reporting, and audit duties. Surveillance device vendors would lose most federal sales of the listed equipment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal agencies and surveillance equipment vendors

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves state and local collection itself untouched, so the cameras and plate readers keep recording everyone; it only regulates when federal agencies can look at the data, and it leaves the private data-sharing market largely alone [S2].

A broad emergency exception lets agency heads acquire data without a warrant when they believe imminent danger requires it, with disposal required within 30 days unless a warrant follows — a gap critics of similar rules have called easy to overuse [S2].

Law enforcement and some prosecutors would argue that warrant-free access to already-collected local data speeds up cases involving fugitives, missing persons, and trafficking, and that the 30-day retention limit and evidence ban could slow legitimate investigations [S2].

The Attorney General controls which technologies go on the covered list and how minimization rules are written, so the practical strength of the protections depends on how the executive branch implements them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: warrantless access to local surveillance data can help solve crimes quickly, but it lets the federal government track people's movements and conversations with no judicial check. The bill keeps emergency access for imminent-danger cases and carves out warrant-based and toll-collection uses, so the cost to ordinary policing is moderate. The bigger weakness is that it does nothing about the underlying collection by state and local agencies or private vendors — it only walls off the federal door to that data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-July 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary and Oversight committees, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Self introduced H.R. 9716 on July 15, 2026, joined by Reps. Crane and Clyde as original cosponsors [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee [S4].
Seven cosponsors, all Republicans, have signed on [S3].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's action history as of the latest record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill has simply sat in committee. If it stays there, federal agencies keep their current warrant-free access to state and local surveillance data, and surveillance vendors keep federal sales.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Keith Self
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require federal warrants for state and local surveillance data and restrict federal funding for the listed devices.

for.name: Reps. Eli Crane and Andrew Clyde
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill in the House.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors are Republicans and no one has voted on or publicly opposed the bill in the record yet, so the partisan shape of the fight has not formed [S3].

industries.industry: Surveillance technology vendors (license plate readers, police cameras, audio monitoring)
industries.note: The bill bars federal money from buying or installing the listed devices, cutting off a growing federal customer base, though carve-outs remain for toll systems, school programs, and warrant-based case-specific use. Their business depends on building dragnet data collections whose privacy costs fall on the public.

Agencies would need federal warrants before tapping state and local surveillance data and would face retention limits, evidence exclusions, audits, and personal liability for violations. They retain emergency and consent exceptions.
The bill leaves their own collection and use of surveillance data untouched, but the federal market for their data shrinks since federal agencies must now get warrants to access it.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this that are referred to two committees with a single-party sponsor and only seven cosponsors rarely reach the floor in the months remaining before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Unless the Judiciary Committee schedules a markup or the bill attracts broader bipartisan support soon, it will most likely expire in committee at the end of this Congress.
